title: Sue Bryce — Day 1 Keynote: Style, Brand and Who You Are Trying to Attract
summary: The business half of Sue Bryce's teaching, and the necessary companion to her posing material: how a photographer who spent ten to fifteen years as 'a nobody' with no nameable genre built a brand that could actually be sold. Her arc runs from retoucher at eighteen through the 1980s glamour boom, into the early-90s collapse when the word 'glamour' itself became unsayable, and out the other side by defining a style first and then spending fifteen years building the service, marketing and pricing around it. The central argument is that craft alone earns nothing - she was shooting her finished style while taking home 400-500 a week - and that the images you display determine the clients you attract, which makes your portfolio a marketing decision rather than an aesthetic one. Practical doctrine covered: the two permitted eyelines, the 'diamond' of a woman's beauty, connection as the thing that actually sells a portrait, the inner-circle multiplier, before-and-after galleries, and why showing only thin young models guarantees you never book anyone else.

steps.action: DEFINE YOUR STYLE FIRST, and make it one you actually want. Until you identify who you are you cannot build a product, a market, a marketing plan or a promotion around it. Her style locked in around 1999 and the brand has not changed since; the following fifteen years went into the business around it, not the look.

SHOW ONLY WHAT YOU WANT TO SHOOT. A site showing only glamour books only glamour - which she chose deliberately, reasoning that with no income there was no downside. She refuses weddings and babies outright. Her instruction: stop doing the work you dislike now, and trust that loving it is what makes an income possible.
KNOW WHAT THE CLIENT ACTUALLY WANTS. After photographing 5,000 women: to look younger, slimmer and gorgeous, and to feel beautiful inside and out. Not one has ever asked to be made wider.

THE IMAGES YOU SHOW DETERMINE THE CLIENTS YOU GET. Her stated reason for not shooting boudoir is market size, not distaste - she estimates it at roughly 3% and rates her own market far larger. Sharper point: a body-led image can repel as easily as attract, because the viewer compares her own body to it and concludes she does not qualify.
EVERYTHING IS ABOUT THE FACE - every other part of the frame drops away. The face shot is a signature shot and CANNOT be cropped in from a wider frame; it must be photographed as its own shot.

TWO EYELINES ONLY: straight down the lens, or down the subject's own body line. Straight into camera reads as 'I am looking at you'; the body line reads as 'I am inside my own energy'. Any other eyeline becomes a model pose rather than a portrait.
Shoot the face straight on, flat lit, with a reflector bouncing back into it. She names the resulting consistency as a feature - same line, same eyeline, same feeling across the whole body of work.

THE DIAMOND: she locates a woman's beauty in the area from the top of the head, out to the outside of the shoulders, down to the base of the decolletage. Never close that diamond down - open and enhance it. Every pose is built to serve it.

DIRECT, DO NOT POSE. A pose is static; she directs - movement, hands touching the body, a look, an eyeline. She argues the sensuality is in the RULES, not the photographer, so anyone can direct it: she was taught by a man, and has taught it to people who do not carry it themselves.

CONNECTION IS WHAT SELLS. When the camera rises, a self-conscious veil drops over the client - mouth stiffens, eyebrows lift, the body locks, expression dies. Removing that is the job. She claims no image in her portfolio lacks direct connection, and that connection, not the pose or the makeup, is what makes a portrait sell.

TARGET MARKET, stated as 'all women aged 8 to 80'. Told that is not a demographic, she insists it is. She does not want to photograph famous or already-photographed people; she wants any woman who has looked in a mirror and not felt good enough, photographed every year of her life so she can see how she looks to other people.

OPEN THE BRAND WITHOUT CHANGING IT. Couples double the sale, but the partner is NOT on the website - she markets to the woman and he arrives with her. Same logic extends to sisters, mothers, best friends and families.

THE INNER CIRCLE MULTIPLIER. Six friends booking a girls' day out is six separate sales in one day. She marks a three-generation shoot as a glamour session while it is functionally a family session, and each woman in it connects to a further network of spouses, children and grandchildren. Women are, in her framing, the most powerful networkers available to a portrait studio.

PUBLISH BEFORE-AND-AFTERS. Traffic to that gallery outperformed everything else. They demonstrate achievability - the transformation is what the culture already consumes everywhere else - and they tell a prospective client concretely what you do. She will retouch or shoot the 'before' with makeup rather than make anyone look bad in it.

ADVERTISE THE CLIENTS YOU WANT. If mothers are not booking, look at whether your advertising shows mothers. Showing only young thin models and wondering why no one else calls is self-inflicted. She refuses the term 'plus size' outright and says 'girls with curves', or simply 'girls'. (She cites model-BMI statistics in support; treat those figures as her claim, not as verified data.)

CRAFT ALONE EARNS NOTHING. She was shooting her finished, recognisable style while taking home 400-500 a week on wages. People do not buy work because it is good; they buy because of how it is presented and sold. Learning to sustain an income is a separate skill from learning to photograph.

STARTED WITH ALMOST NOTHING: a Canon 10D, a single 24-105, a laptop, no tablet, a converted four-car garage half an hour outside the city, and 3,000 borrowed from her parents. Fifteen weeks later the business had earned 20,000. She stresses no marketing degree, no business degree, no formal photography training.

THE BLOCKED-ARTIST TRAP, which she admits to having lived in for years: sitting at a computer browsing competitors' sites thinking 'I do not understand why they are successful when I am clearly more talented.' She names that as the voice of a blocked artist criticising the people who are actually out there doing it. The remedy is to take action.

VALUE YOUR OWN TIME FIRST. Her philosophy, set into the floor of the studio she built: until you honour and value your time and yourself, you will not be paid or honoured for it, because you do not honour it yourself. She reads Derek Walcott's poem 'Love After Love' as the statement of it - look the poem up rather than storing it here.

PRICING outcome: a simplified price list built to be easy to buy from, an 1,800 average sale from a single client at the studio, and 3,300 working on her own in Sydney. Paul Arden's line, that talent takes you far but ambition takes you further, is the framing she keeps on the wall.

key_takeaways: Define the style FIRST; the business, marketing and pricing get built around it afterwards. Until you can say who you are, there is nothing to market.
Your portfolio is a marketing decision, not an aesthetic one - the images you display are the only thing determining who calls you.
Craft does not produce income. She shot her finished style for years while earning wages, because selling and presenting are separate skills from photographing.
Everything serves the face, and the face shot must be photographed as its own shot - it cannot be cropped in from a wider frame.
Two eyelines only: straight down the lens, or down the subject's own body line. Anything else turns a portrait into a model pose.
The 'diamond' - head to outer shoulders to base of decolletage - is where she locates beauty, and every pose opens it rather than closing it down.
Connection is what sells a portrait. The camera rising makes a client self-conscious and kills the expression; removing that veil is the actual work.
Sell to the inner circle: one booking becomes six sales in a day, and each woman connects to a wider family network worth far more than the original session.
Advertise the client you want to book. Showing only thin young models and wondering why mothers or curvy women never call is self-inflicted.
Before-and-afters outperform everything because they prove achievability - they tell a prospect she qualifies.
